passage:
Dear Diary,
Two new boys came to our class today. Pranjal has round glasses and hardly speaks. He is definitely going to be the topper. You can just tell. Zubin is loud and made the whole back row laugh when Miss was writing on the board, so he must be weak in studies. I chose Pranjal as my partner for the maths quiz. Then Pranjal got three sums wrong, and Zubin got all of them right and even helped me with the last one. I think Zubin was lucky. Tomorrow I will see.
Afreen

qa.q: Who got all the quiz sums right?
qa.a: Zubin got all of them right and even helped with the last one.

qa.q: Why was Afreen so sure Pranjal would be the topper?
qa.a: Afreen felt confident because Pranjal's round glasses and quietness matched Afreen's picture of a topper, so the look felt like proof even before any test.

qa.q: What could Afreen try tomorrow?
qa.a: Afreen could wait to judge until seeing how each boy actually works over a few days, and notice that the quiz already gave real evidence about Zubin.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel if he knew Afreen called him lucky?
qa.a: Zubin might feel unfairly judged, since he got every sum right and even helped, yet was still seen as weak because he is loud.

grounding: Shows a child assuming the quiet boy with glasses is the topper and the loud boy is weak, then explaining away the quiz result.

passage: At the village school near Sikar, Masterji asked the class to choose two children for the district quiz. Preeti didn't even think. "Mukesh," she said, pointing to the thin boy with thick glasses who sat quietly by the window. Everyone knew clever people looked like that. When someone suggested Vijay, she wrinkled her nose. Vijay was the one who shouted answers without raising his hand and played kabaddi every break. "He only makes noise," she whispered. Masterji held a practice round under the neem tree. Vijay answered eight questions; Mukesh answered two and blushed. Preeti frowned at the chalk tally, as if it had made a mistake.

qa.q: How many questions did Vijay answer in the practice round?
qa.a: Vijay answered eight questions.

qa.q: Why did Preeti frown at the chalk tally?
qa.a: Preeti feels puzzled and a little annoyed, because she had been sure Mukesh's glasses and quietness meant he was clever and Vijay's noise meant he was weak. The tally feels wrong to her rather than informative.

qa.q: How could Masterji help the class choose fairly?
qa.a: Masterji could pick the team from practice rounds like this one and point out that answers, not looks or loudness, show who knows the material.

qa.q: How might Mukesh feel being picked first and then answering only two?
qa.a: Mukesh may feel embarrassed and under pressure, since he was chosen for how he looks rather than for what he knows.

grounding: Shows a child assuming the quiet boy with glasses must be clever and the loud boy weak, until a practice round disagrees.

passage: On the first day of fourth grade in Kraków, Olga whispered to her friend Ines, "The boy with the glasses, Tomek, he must be a genius. Look how quietly he sits." Ines shrugged. "And that one?" She pointed at Filip, who was drumming on the desk and telling a joke about the teacher's cat. "Definitely bad at maths," Olga said. By Friday the class had done its first test. Filip had the top mark and got a sticker. Tomek had struggled, and at break he told Olga he hated numbers and loved drawing birds. Olga stared at the sticker on Filip's hand for a long time.

qa.q: Who got the top mark in the first test?
qa.a: Filip had the top mark and got a sticker.

qa.q: Why did Olga decide Tomek must be a genius?
qa.a: Olga felt confident because Tomek wore glasses and sat quietly, which matched her picture of a clever child, so his look felt like enough evidence.

qa.q: What could Olga do the next time she meets new classmates?
qa.a: Olga could notice the guess, then wait for real signs, like tests, what people say they love, or how they solve problems, before deciding who is clever.

qa.q: What might Tomek feel if he knew what Olga had first assumed?
qa.a: Tomek might feel pressure or awkwardness at being expected to be a genius at something he dislikes, when what he loves is drawing birds.

grounding: Shows a child judging a quiet boy with glasses as a genius and a loud boy as weak at maths, until the first test shows otherwise.

passage: On day one of the summer chess camp at the community centre, the coach said, "Pick a partner for the puzzle relay." Nilesh, eight, didn't hesitate. He walked straight to Tarun, a thin, quiet boy with big round glasses who was reading the rules sheet. "He looks like a topper," Nilesh whispered to himself. Sonu, a loud boy who had been bouncing a ball, came up hopefully. Nilesh shook his head. "You're too noisy for chess." The relay began. Tarun stared at the first puzzle for ages and got it wrong. At the next table, Sonu shouted "Checkmate!" and slammed down the knight, the fastest in the room. Nilesh's mouth dropped open. At lunch, he went and sat next to Sonu. "How did you see that knight move?"

qa.q: How did Sonu's pair do in the relay?
qa.a: Sonu shouted "Checkmate!" and was the fastest in the room.

qa.q: Why was Nilesh so sure Tarun would be good at chess?
qa.a: Nilesh felt confident because Tarun was quiet, read the rules and wore big round glasses, matching his picture of a topper. The look felt like enough proof.

qa.q: What choice did Nilesh make at lunch, and why was it a good one?
qa.a: He sat next to Sonu and asked how he saw the knight move. That let him learn about Sonu from what Sonu actually did, not from how loud he was.

qa.q: How might Sonu have felt when Nilesh said he was too noisy for chess?
qa.a: Sonu probably felt hurt and left out, being judged before playing a single move.

grounding: A boy at chess camp picks a quiet boy with glasses as his partner because he looks clever, and refuses a loud boy who turns out to be the best.

passage: I'm Nandini, and I help run the Sunday maths club in our building's hall. Here's what I saw with Farida, who's ten. We were forming teams for the number puzzles. Farida marched up to Pranit, who wears thick glasses and barely speaks, and said, "You're with me." Then Gogi, who is loud and was doing cartwheels near the door, asked to join. Farida said, "No thanks, you'll just mess around." I don't know exactly what was in her head. But she kept glancing at Pranit's glasses like they were a guarantee. In the round, Pranit froze; he'd never done this kind of puzzle. Gogi, on another team, finished first and whooped. Farida went red. Later I saw her ask Gogi to show her his trick. Maybe she learned something.

qa.q: What was Gogi doing near the door when he asked to join?
qa.a: He was doing cartwheels near the door.

qa.q: Why might Farida have thought Pranit was a guarantee?
qa.a: He looked like her idea of a clever child, with thick glasses and a quiet manner, so choosing him felt safe. Gogi's loudness seemed to mean he would not be serious.

qa.q: After the round, what did Farida choose to do, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She asked Gogi to show her his trick. That shows she was willing to learn from what she saw rather than stick to her first guess.

qa.q: How might Pranit feel being picked because of his glasses?
qa.a: Pranit may feel pressure to be a genius and embarrassed when he freezes, since he had never done this kind of puzzle.

grounding: A maths club helper describes a girl at a maths club who picks a quiet boy with glasses as her partner and turns away a loud boy who then wins.
